title: How to Replace a Faucet Aerator
summary: This Old House demonstrates diagnosing and addressing a clogged faucet aerator. The host explains that aerators incorporate a flow restrictor and can accumulate debris that reduces water pressure. The tutorial covers removing the aerator with an adjustable wrench, inspecting and cleaning the interior (noting debris such as coffee grounds), and deciding to replace the aerator rather than clean it when debris buildup is significant. A replacement cost hint (~$5–$6) is given, followed by a hot-and-cold water test to confirm proper function after replacement.

sections.title: Aerator function and symptoms of blockage
sections.description: The video explains that aerators were designed to create a clearer stream and conserve water via a flow restrictor that funnels all water through a small hole. The host suggests debris between the flow path and the aerator can cause partial or complete flow shutoff, setting up the diagnostic moment.

sections.title: Removing the aerator with an adjustable wrench
sections.description: To remove the aerator, the presenter uses an adjustable open-end wrench on the two flat edges, taking care to avoid scratching if the aerator is round and noting that some fittings are only hand-tight.

sections.title: Inspecting interior and debris cleaning
sections.description: Upon inspection, a buildup of debris (described as coffee grinds) is found inside the aerator. The host flushes the spout with a rag to evaluate whether cleaning alone will restore proper flow.

sections.title: Replacement decision and final test
sections.description: The presenter decides to replace the aerator due to significant debris, cites a rough replacement cost of $5–$6, and performs a hot-and-cold water test to confirm both flows are functioning after replacement.
